latin.2546: CVIII. Porro ex dictis facile colligitur recentiorum Thomistarum doctrinam, quam exponit Didacus Alvarez, e diametro oppositam esse doctrinae quam tradit Molina, circa gratiam illam quae dicitur efficax, & cui tribuitur hominis conversio. Prorsus enim inter se pugnant, sive spectetur modus quo gratia hominem movet ad actus quibus ad Deum convertitur, sive natura ipsa & quidditas gratiae, & qua in re illa ponenda est.
latin.2547: CIX. Nam quod attinet ad modum operandi gratiae, Thomistae recentiores, ut Didacus Alvarez, volunt gratiam illam per quam homo convertitur, esse efficacem per se, neque talem reddi per liberi arbitrii consensum, sed illa potenter & infallibiliter liberum arbitrium ad consensum determinari; sicut ante fuit expositum. Contra vero Molina, & qui eum sequuntur, pertendunt gratiam quae hominem convertit, ita libero arbitrio subjici, ut efficacia ejus a consensu liberi arbitrii pendeat, & sit in libera hominis potestate illam vel efficacem, vel inefficacem reddere, quorum utrumque de facto saepius eveniat.
latin.2548: CX. Quod spectat autem essentiam gratiae, qua movetur voluntas ad actus conversionis, & quae conversionem reipsa operatur, Recentiores Thomistae illam ponunt ut supra dictum, in motione aliqua virtuosa, quae habet esse quoddam incompletum, & est in voluntate per modum quo colores sunt in aere, & impetus in re quae impellitur. Molina vero gratiam quae, consentiente libero arbitrio, hominem efficaciter movet ad conversionem, ponit in affectibus quibusdam voluntatis, ex praevia mentis illuminatione ortis, quibus Deus per suum influxum se inserens, allicit voluntatem ut velit, & vires volendi tribuit, simulque concurrit cum voluntate si voluerit.
latin.2549: CXI. Proinde hac in parte propius a Molina Jansenius distat quam Thomistae recentiores. Quanquam enim cum illis Jansenius prorsus consentiat circa modum operandi gratiae efficacis, contendens efficaciam salutaris Christi gratiae nullatenus a consensu arbitrii humani pendere, sed consensum illum per se efficere, idque infallibiliter & insuperabiliter; nihilominus quod spectat naturam & substantiam gratiae quae dicitur efficax, minus abest ejus sententia a doctrina Molinae, quam a Doctrina Thomistarum. Quippe, ut ex antedictis manifestum est, gratiam illam efficacem, cui, juxta ipsum, hominis conversio, & omnia bona fidelium opera in solidum tribui debent, constituit in quibusdam affectibus amoris & desiderii, qui ab hominis voluntate, non libere quidem, sed active procedunt, ejusque sunt actus vitales, & quibus voluntas ad bonum libere amplectendum fertur & inducitur. Tales enim affectus intelligit nomine coelestis suavitatis & delectationis, in qua gratiam efficacem ponit.
latin.2550: CXII. Verum in eo differt a Molina, quod affectus istiusmodi, secundum Molinae doctrinam, mere naturaliter in voluntate oriuntur, posita mentis illuminatione: nec aliud praestat Deus, quam quod affectibus illis peculiari influxu se ingerit, eosque reddit supernaturales. Juxta Jansenium vero, posita quacunque mentis illuminatione, affectus isti in hominis corrupti voluntate per naturam non exurgunt, sed necesse est illos totos coelitus immitti, non simpliciter quadam divina motione acui, & intendi, ut fiant supernaturales.
latin.2551: CXIV. Praeterea Molina ad naturam voluntatis absolute consideratae pertinere existimat, ut statim atque intellectus aliquod objectum ipsi offert ut bonum & delectabile, erga illud motu quodam afficiatur, & tangatur affectu, qui voluntatem illicit & proritat, ut tale objectum libere amplectatur. Nec putat voluntatem in objectum aliquod ut bonum libere ferri, quin ejusmodi motus & affectus naturaliter exoriens in ea praecesserit. Adeoque quum homo, & Angelus integer, a vero bono declinare coepit, & terrenum ac privatum bonum spirituali & divino praeferre, in utroque malam voluntatem, juxta ipsum, antecessit ejusmodi motus & affectus, quo homo ad pomum vetitum comedendum, Angelus ad propriam excellentiam admirandam atque suspiciendam, excitabatur & alliciebatur.
latin.2552: CXV. Jansenius autem illum amorem & desiderium, quod delectationis nomine significat, & quo voluntas jam trahitur, priusquam quicquam libere velit & amplectatur, ac quo praesertim illam affici necesse est, antequam prosequatur bonum coeleste & spirituale, necessario praecedere non censet omnes voluntatis actus, si consideretur absolute, & citra infirmitatem per peccatum contractam. Etenim secundum illius doctrinam, non est simpliciter de natura voluntatis, ut non valeat libere bonum objectum amplecti, nisi prius delectaverit: ac multo minus ad naturam voluntatis pertinet, ut si objectum bonum & jucundum ipsi offeratur, tangatur aliqua delectatione. Praesertim vero docet peccatum primum sive hominum, sive Angelorum, sine delectatione praecedenti perpetratum esse: nec ullum fuisse vel in hominibus, vel in angelis integris affectum, quo ad primum malum voluntatis actum sollicitati & invitati sint.

sections.title: The recent Thomists and Molina diametrically opposed
sections.pass_a: CVIII. Moreover from what has been said it is easily gathered that the doctrine of the recent Thomists, which Didacus Alvarez sets out, is diametrically opposed to the doctrine which Molina teaches, concerning that grace which is called efficacious, & to which the conversion of man is attributed. For they fight altogether among themselves, whether the manner be regarded by which grace moves man to the acts by which he is converted to God, or the very nature & quiddity of grace, & in what thing it is to be placed.
pass_b: Thesis CVIII. From all this it is easy to see that the doctrine of the recent Thomists, as Diego Alvarez presents it, stands diametrically opposed to Molina's teaching about the grace called efficacious, the grace to which a person's conversion is ascribed. The two are in complete conflict, whether we look at the way grace moves a person to the acts by which he turns to God, or at the nature and quiddity of grace itself and where it is to be located.

sections.title: On how grace works: efficacious of itself, or by consent
sections.pass_a: CIX. For as regards the manner of operating of grace, the recent Thomists, as Didacus Alvarez, will have that grace by which man is converted, to be efficacious of itself, nor to be rendered such by the consent of free choice, but free choice to be determined by it powerfully & infallibly to consent; as was set out before. But on the contrary Molina, & those who follow him, contend that the grace which converts man, is so subjected to free choice, that its efficacy depends on the consent of free choice, & it is in man's free power to render it either efficacious, or inefficacious, both of which in fact quite often happen.
pass_b: Thesis CIX. On the way grace works, the recent Thomists, Alvarez among them, hold that the grace by which a person is converted is efficacious of itself. It is not made so by the consent of free choice; rather, as was explained earlier, it determines free choice to consent, powerfully and infallibly.

Molina and his followers maintain the opposite: the grace that converts a person is subject to free choice in such a way that its efficacy depends on free choice's consent. It lies in a person's free power to make it efficacious or inefficacious, and in fact each of these quite often happens.

sections.title: On what grace is: a virtual motion, or affections of the will
sections.pass_a: CX. But as regards the essence of grace, by which the will is moved to the acts of conversion, & which in very fact works conversion, the Recent Thomists place it as was said above, in some virtual motion, which has a certain incomplete being, & is in the will in the way in which colours are in the air, & impetus in a thing which is impelled. But Molina places the grace which, free choice consenting, moves man efficaciously to conversion, in certain affections of the will, arisen from a previous illumination of the mind, into which God inserting himself by his influx, entices the will to will, & gives the strength of willing, and at the same time concurs with the will if it will.
pass_b: Thesis CX. As for the essence of the grace by which the will is moved to the acts of conversion and which actually brings conversion about, the recent Thomists, as was said above, place it in a virtual motion. This motion has an incomplete kind of being and is in the will as colours are in the air, or as impetus is in a thing that is being driven along.

Molina places the grace that moves a person efficaciously to conversion, when free choice consents, in certain affections of the will that arise from a prior illumination of the mind. God inserts himself into them by his influence, draws the will to will, gives it the strength to will, and concurs with the will at the same time, if it wills.

sections.title: Jansenius nearer Molina than the Thomists on the nature of grace
sections.pass_a: CXI. Therefore in this part Jansenius stands nearer to Molina than the recent Thomists. For although Jansenius agrees altogether with them about the manner of operating of efficacious grace, contending that the efficacy of Christ's saving grace in no way depends on the consent of human choice, but effects that consent of itself, and that infallibly & insuperably; nevertheless as regards the nature & substance of the grace which is called efficacious, his opinion is less distant from the doctrine of Molina, than from the Doctrine of the Thomists. Since, as is manifest from what was said before, that efficacious grace, to which, according to him, the conversion of man, & all the good works of the faithful ought to be attributed in full, he places in certain affections of love & desire, which proceed from man's will, not freely indeed, but actively, & are its vital acts, & by which the will is borne & led to embrace the good freely. For such affections he understands by the name of heavenly sweetness & delight, in which he places efficacious grace.
pass_b: Thesis CXI. On this point, then, Jansenius stands closer to Molina than the recent Thomists do. He agrees with the Thomists entirely on the way efficacious grace works, contending that the efficacy of Christ's saving grace in no way depends on the consent of human choice but produces that consent of itself, infallibly and insuperably. Yet on the nature and substance of the grace called efficacious, his view is less far from Molina's doctrine than from the Thomists'.

As is clear from what was said earlier, he places this efficacious grace, to which in his view a person's conversion and all the good works of the faithful must be wholly ascribed, in certain affections of love and desire. These proceed from the human will, not freely but actively; they are its vital acts, and by them the will is carried and led to embrace the good freely. Such are the affections he means by the name of heavenly sweetness and delight, in which he places efficacious grace.

sections.title: Where Jansenius differs from Molina: natural affections or heaven-sent
sections.pass_a: CXII. But he differs from Molina in this, that affections of this kind, according to Molina's doctrine, arise merely naturally in the will, illumination of the mind being posited: nor does God do anything else, than that he thrusts himself into those affections by a peculiar influx, and renders them supernatural. But according to Jansenius, any illumination of the mind whatever being posited, those affections do not rise up by nature in the will of corrupt man, but it is necessary that they be sent in wholly from heaven, not simply sharpened & intensified by some divine motion, that they may become supernatural.
pass_b: Thesis CXII. He differs from Molina, however, in this. On Molina's doctrine such affections arise in the will purely by nature once the mind is illuminated, and God does no more than thrust himself into them by a special influence and make them supernatural.

On Jansenius's view, whatever illumination of the mind is given, these affections do not rise by nature in the will of fallen man. They must be sent into it wholly from heaven, and not merely sharpened and heightened by some divine motion so as to become supernatural.

sections.title: Molina: a natural affection precedes every free act of the will
sections.pass_a: CXIV. Moreover Molina thinks it pertains to the nature of the will considered absolutely, that as soon as the intellect offers it some object as good & delightful, it is affected toward it by a certain motion, & is touched by an affection, which entices & provokes the will, so that it freely embraces such an object. Nor does he think that the will is freely borne toward any object as good, without such a motion & affection, arising naturally in it, having preceded. And so when man, & the Angel unfallen, began to decline from the true good, & to prefer an earthly and private good to the spiritual & divine, in both, according to him, such a motion & affection preceded the evil will, by which man was excited & allured to eating the forbidden apple, the Angel to admiring & looking up to his own excellence.
pass_b: Thesis CXIV. Molina further holds that it belongs to the nature of the will, considered absolutely, that as soon as the intellect presents it with some object as good and delightful, it is moved toward that object by a certain motion and touched by an affection. That affection entices and provokes the will to embrace such an object freely. He does not think the will is ever borne freely toward any object as good unless a motion and affection of this kind, arising naturally in it, has gone before.

So when man and the angel, still unfallen, began to turn away from the true good and to prefer an earthly, private good to the spiritual and divine, in each case, on his view, the evil will was preceded by such a motion and affection. By it the man was roused and drawn to eat the forbidden fruit, and the angel to admire and look up to his own excellence.

sections.title: Jansenius: delight is not of the will's nature, nor preceded the first sin
sections.pass_a: CXV. But Jansenius does not think that that love & desire, which he signifies by the name of delight, & by which the will is now drawn, before it freely wills & embraces anything, and with which above all it must be affected, before it pursues the heavenly & spiritual good, necessarily precedes all acts of the will, if it be considered absolutely, & apart from the infirmity contracted through sin. For according to his doctrine, it is not simply of the nature of the will, that it cannot freely embrace a good object, unless it has first delighted: and much less does it pertain to the nature of the will, that if a good & pleasant object be offered to it, it be touched by some delight. But above all he teaches that the first sin whether of men, or of Angels, was committed without preceding delight: nor was there any affection either in men, or in the unfallen angels, by which they were solicited & invited to the first evil act of the will.
pass_b: Thesis CXV. Jansenius, by contrast, does not hold that the love and desire he calls delight necessarily precede every act of the will, when the will is considered absolutely and apart from the weakness contracted through sin. This is the delight by which the will is now drawn before it freely wills and embraces anything, and by which above all it must be touched before it pursues the heavenly and spiritual good.

On his doctrine it is not simply part of the will's nature that it cannot freely embrace a good object unless the object has first delighted it. Still less does it belong to the will's nature to be touched by some delight whenever a good and pleasant object is presented to it. Above all, he teaches that the first sin, of men and of angels alike, was committed without any preceding delight, and that neither men nor angels in their unfallen state had any affection by which they were solicited and invited to the will's first evil act.
